KEY MESSAGE 1... As of 12:45 AM EST...Current satellite imagery 
shows high clouds just starting to increase across western portions 
of our region, with some stratus moving up from the south towards 
the I-84 corridor. While more sheltered areas that were able to 
decouple have seen temps drop into the upper 40s so far this 
evening, the rest of the region remains well into the 50s to low low 
60s, which is quite warm for this time of year. Temperatures won't 
drop much from current levels through the rest of the night with 
increasing clouds.

As we head towards daybreak, a sfc low tracking into southern Canada 
will drag its attendant cold front through the region. Deep 
southerly flow with a connection to the Gulf will allow PWATs to 
surge to around 1.5" ahead of the front, which is around 3 std dev 
above normal for early November. However, the best upper forcing and 
dynamics will remain to the west of our region so the area of 
showers associated with the cold front is expected to gradually 
weaken as it tracks through the region. This will be especially true 
for the Capital District and Mid Hudson Valley where southwest low 
to mid-level winds will downslope off of the Catskills. For most of 
the region, a tenth to quarter inch of qpf is expected through 
Thursday evening, but upslope flow into the southern ADKs will lead 
to higher qpf here closer to a half to three quarters of an inch. 
This rain is much-needed given that that is has been almost 3 weeks 
since most of the region saw appreciable rainfall. Tomorrow will be 
about 5-10 degrees cooler than Wednesday was, but temperatures will 
still be above normal with relatively high humidity (at least by 
November standards). Tomorrow also looks breezy, with wind gusts up 
to 20 to possibly 30 mph, strongest out ahead of the front and in 
the N/S oriented valleys due to flow channeling.

Tomorrow night, the front will stall off to the east of our region 
with some scattered showers continuing across southeastern areas. 
Just how far to the east it stall remains a point of forecast 
uncertainty, however, and will have large implications as to whether 
or not we see another round of rain Friday and Friday night. During 
this time period, the parent ULL will be slowly drifting across the 
southern Great Lakes region, with a southern stream shortwave 
expected to track around its southern periphery and become 
negatively tilted as it moves over the East Coast. This will result 
in the development of a wave of low pressure along the stalled 
frontal boundary. With continued moisture advection and convergence 
along the front, this will lead to a band of moderate to at times 
heavy rain developing Friday into Friday night. At this time, the 
consensus is that the front will stall far enough to our east that 
most of our region will miss out on this rain, although Litchfield
County and the southern Mid Hudson Valley will likely see at
least some rain. Wherever this area of rain sets up, it looks 
like there will be a sharp QPF gradient on the W/NW side of the 
band. The latest NBM has a 30-40% chance for >0.5" of rain 
southeast of Rte 202 in Litchfield County, with only a 10-20% 
chance for areas north and west. Temperatures remains several 
degrees above normal Thursday night through Friday night. 


KEY MESSAGE 2... Regardless of how the Friday/Friday night system 
evolves, confidence is beginning to increase for another round of 
showers Saturday afternoon and night into early Sunday. The parent 
ULL will slowly drift over our region, and while there remains some 
uncertainty in its track, general consensus seems for it to track 
somewhere in the vicinity or just south of the I-90 corridor. Fairly 
widespread showers are expected Saturday, especially under the ULL 
and on the NW side where the best upper deformation will be. 
Additionally, there are signals for an inverted sfc trough to 
develop extending westwards from the deepening coastal low to the 
ULL, which will likely act to locally enhance shower coverage and 
intensity wherever it sets up across our region. NBM suggests a 20-
30% for >0.5" of additional rain across the Mid Hudson Valley with a 
30-50% chance across the rest of the region, but would not be 
surprised to see these probabilities increase over the next day or 
two with many deterministic sources of guidance suggesting some 
amounts in excess of 1" are possible where the most persistent and 
heaviest showers set up. Even if rainfall totals end up higher
than the current forecast, we have no hydro concerns at all 
given very dry antecedent conditions. 

Showers come to an end Sunday morning as the ULL drifts off the east 
coast. A few snow flakes could mix in over the highest terrain of 
the ADKs before precip comes to an end Sunday morning. Cooler, but
